stem: A 22-year-old woman has 3 days of migrating joint pain, tender swollen tendon sheaths at the wrists, and a few pustules on her hands. Gram stain of joint fluid shows gram-negative diplococci. At 16 she had meningococcal meningitis. Her CH50 is nearly zero, while C3 and C4 levels are normal, and she has had no other unusual infections.
oneliner: 22F + migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis, pustules + joint fluid gram-negative diplococci + meningococcal meningitis at 16 + CH50 near zero + normal C3, C4 + no other unusual infections → which defect?
ask: Which defect most likely explains her recurrent Neisseria infections?

options.C: Absence of a late complement component that forms the membrane attack complex

whyNot.A: **Hereditary angioedema**: recurrent swelling, low C4, not Neisseria infections
whyNot.B: **C3 deficiency**: severe recurrent pyogenic infections of many organisms, with low C3
whyNot.D: **C4** lack gives a **lupus-like** illness with low C4
whyNot.E: **PNH**: complement-mediated hemolysis and thrombosis, not Neisseria infection

answer: C5-C9 deficiency (no membrane attack complex)
why: **Recurrent Neisseria infections with CH50 near zero and normal C3 and C4** means a **late (C5-C9) deficiency**. Without the **membrane attack complex**, the **only defence against encapsulated Neisseria, lysis**, is lost, so bacteria disseminate.

idea.rule: Recurrent Neisseria infection means think terminal complement (C5-C9) deficiency; CH50 is absent but C3 and C4 are normal.
also: Vaccinate against meningococcus; give prophylaxis
C3 deficiency: recurrent bacterial infections with immune complex disease
Early classical component deficiency (C1q, C2, C4): lupus-like

stem: A 27-year-old woman has sneezing fits, clear watery nasal discharge, and itchy red eyes every spring, worst after gardening. She has no fever or facial pain. A stained smear of her nasal secretions is examined during a flare.
oneliner: 27F + sneezing, clear rhinorrhea, itchy eyes every spring + worse gardening + no fever or facial pain + nasal smear in flare → which cell predominates?
ask: Which cell type is most likely increased in her nasal smear?

whyNot.A: Seen in **bacterial sinusitis** with pus and fever
whyNot.B: Suggest **viral** rhinitis (fever, malaise); she is afebrile with a seasonal pattern
whyNot.C: Make antibody **within the tissue**; not shed as the characteristic cell
whyNot.D: Release histamine too but are **scant**; eosinophils dominate the allergic smear

answer: Eosinophils recruited by IL-5 after mast cell activation
why: Pollen **cross-links IgE on mast cells**, causing **degranulation** (histamine, sneezing, itch). **Th2 cytokines, IL-5 and eotaxin**, then recruit **eosinophils** into the nasal mucosa and secretions, the characteristic cell on smear.
chain: Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells
Th2 cells release IL-4 and IL-5

idea.rule: Eosinophils mark allergic (type I) inflammation and parasitic infection; neutrophils mark bacterial infection.
also: IL-4 and IL-13 switch B cells to IgE
IL-5 drives eosinophil production
Asthma and atopic dermatitis share this pathway

stem: In cell culture, a virus lowers MHC class I expression on the mouse cells it infects. These infected cells are killed in the dish by lymphocytes taken from the blood of mice with no prior exposure to the virus. Killing occurs within hours.
oneliner: Culture: virus lowers MHC I on infected cells + killed within hours by lymphocytes from unexposed mice → which cell and why?
ask: Which cell most likely kills the infected cells, and why?

options.A: CD8 T cells, because they recognize viral peptide on MHC class I
options.B: Natural killer cells, because they attack cells that lack MHC class I
options.C: CD4 T cells, because they recognize peptide on MHC class II
options.D: Plasma cells, because they secrete antibody
options.E: Follicular dendritic cells, because they present antigen to B cells

whyNot.A: CD8 cells **need MHC I to see antigen**, and naive cells take days to expand
whyNot.C: CD4 cells **help** other cells and **do not kill** infected cells directly
whyNot.D: Antibody production takes **days** and needs a prior response
whyNot.E: They **trap antigen in germinal centres**; they do not kill cells

answer: NK cells detecting missing self
why: **NK cells carry inhibitory receptors for MHC class I**. When a virus **removes MHC I**, the brake is lost and NK cells **release perforin and granzymes**, killing the cell **within hours and without prior exposure**.
chain: CD8 T cells cannot see antigen
NK inhibitory receptors lose their signal

idea.rule: Missing self (low MHC I) triggers NK killing; present self with foreign peptide triggers CD8 killing.
also: CMV and HIV Nef lower MHC I
NK cells also use ADCC via CD16
Tumor cells that lose MHC I are also NK targets

stem: A 78-year-old man dies after several years of congestive heart failure with low cardiac output. At autopsy, a photomicrograph of the kidney is shown. The nuclei look normal, and there is no inflammation.
oneliner: 78M + chronic CHF, low output + autopsy kidney micrograph shown + nuclei normal, no inflammation → mechanism of the change?
ask: Which mechanism most likely produced the changes seen?

options.A: Failure of the Na+/K+-ATPase pump from ATP depletion
options.C: Fall in intracellular pH from lactic acid
options.D: Impaired protein synthesis from ribosome detachment

whyNot.B: Calcium rise activates enzymes and signals **irreversible** injury, with nuclear change
whyNot.C: Lactic acid causes **chromatin clumping**; it is not what swells the cell
whyNot.D: Ribosomal detachment makes cells **less basophilic** but does not cause swelling
whyNot.E: **Irreversible** injury shows nuclear pyknosis, karyolysis; the nuclei here are normal

answer: Hydropic change: ATP depletion, pump failure, Na+ and water influx
why: **Low cardiac output causes renal hypoxia**, so **ATP falls**. The **Na+/K+-ATPase fails**, sodium and water enter, and the **tubular cells swell and look pale and vacuolated**. This **reversible change** keeps normal nuclei.

idea.rule: Cell swelling is the first and reversible sign of hypoxic injury; nuclear change and membrane loss mean irreversible injury.
also: Other early changes: blebbing, ribosome detachment, fatty change
Irreversible: pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis, membrane rupture
Proximal tubule is highly vulnerable to ischemia

image.prompt: Photomicrograph of kidney cortex, H&E: proximal tubular epithelial cells that are swollen, pale, and finely vacuolated, narrowing the tubular lumens. Nuclei are round and intact and there is no inflammatory infiltrate or necrosis. No text or labels.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has pain and swelling of the right arm, and duplex shows thrombosis of the axillary vein. She has had two second-trimester pregnancy losses. Platelets are mildly low, the aPTT is prolonged and does not correct when mixed with normal plasma, and she is not taking an anticoagulant.
oneliner: 33F + arm vein thrombosis + two second-trimester losses + low platelets + prolonged aPTT not correcting on mixing → why thrombosis?
ask: Which of the following best explains her thrombosis and fetal loss?

options.C: Antibodies to phospholipid-binding proteins that activate endothelium and platelets

whyNot.A: Gives thrombosis and warfarin skin necrosis but a **normal aPTT** and no antibody
whyNot.B: Same **normal aPTT**; does not explain a **non-correcting** mixing study
whyNot.D: Causes **heparin resistance** and **normal aPTT**
whyNot.E: Dysfibrinogenemia gives **prolonged thrombin time** and often **bleeding**

answer: Antibodies activate endothelium and platelets in vivo but block phospholipid in vitro
why: **Antiphospholipid antibodies** (anticardiolipin, **β2-glycoprotein I**, lupus anticoagulant) are **prothrombotic** in vivo, causing **thrombosis and placental infarcts**. In vitro they bind the phospholipid in the aPTT reagent, **prolonging** the test without correction.

idea.rule: Prolonged aPTT with thrombosis (not bleeding) and pregnancy loss means antiphospholipid syndrome.
also: Arterial events too: stroke in a young adult
Associated with SLE and a false-positive VDRL/RPR
Lupus anticoagulant prolongs clotting tests yet causes clots

stem: A 40-year-old man had an allogeneic bone marrow transplant from an HLA-mismatched unrelated donor 3 weeks ago. He now has a maculopapular rash on his palms and soles, watery diarrhea, and a rising bilirubin.
oneliner: 40M + bone marrow transplant from unrelated donor 3 wk ago + palm and sole rash + watery diarrhea + high bilirubin → which cells cause it?
ask: Which of the following cell types most likely mediates his condition?

whyNot.A: Antibody makers; **not the main effectors** of graft-versus-host injury
whyNot.B: **Antigen presenters**, not the main killers
whyNot.C: Part of the innate response, not the **donor-derived** attackers
whyNot.E: Innate bacterial responders, **not** in this immune attack

answer: Donor T cells recognize recipient HLA and attack
why: **Graft-versus-host disease** occurs when **mature T cells in the graft** recognize the host's **HLA as foreign** and attack the **skin, gut and liver**, causing rash, diarrhea and hepatitis.
chain: Donor T cells in the marrow graft
Attack skin, gut and bile ducts

idea.rule: Graft-versus-host disease is a T-cell attack by the donor graft on the immunocompromised host.
also: Prevent with HLA matching and T-cell depletion of the graft; treat with steroids
GVHD brings a beneficial graft-versus-leukemia effect
Requires an immunocompromised host, immunocompetent donor cells, and HLA difference

stem: A 22-year-old man has had several episodes of swelling of the lips and tongue, the last after a dental extraction. The swelling is not itchy, there is no hives and it does not respond to epinephrine or antihistamines. He has also had colicky abdominal pain. He takes no medications, and his C4 level is low.
oneliner: 22M + lip and tongue swelling after dental extraction + no itch or hives + no response to epinephrine or antihistamine + colicky pain + low C4 → which mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best explains his episodes?

options.C: Unchecked bradykinin from C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency
options.D: Deficiency of a heme synthesis enzyme

whyNot.A: **Allergy**: itchy, urticarial and **responds to epinephrine**
whyNot.B: **Familial Mediterranean fever**: fever, serositis; no swelling
whyNot.D: **Acute porphyria**: abdominal pain, neurologic signs, but no swelling
whyNot.E: **Toxic shock**: fever, hypotension and rash

answer: C1 inhibitor deficiency causes excess bradykinin
why: **C1 esterase inhibitor** normally restrains **kallikrein, factor XII and C1**. When it is missing, **bradykinin** accumulates and increases **vascular permeability**, causing nonpitting swelling without itch or response to antihistamines, with **low C4** between and during attacks.
chain: Nonpruritic angioedema and gut wall swelling

idea.rule: Angioedema without itch or hives that does not respond to epinephrine or antihistamines is bradykinin-mediated.
also: ACE inhibitors cause the same swelling by blocking bradykinin breakdown
Acute attack treatment: icatibant (bradykinin B2 blocker), C1 inhibitor concentrate
Low C4 screens for HAE

stem: A 6-year-old girl has had repeated skin and liver abscesses with Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia and Burkholderia. She handles viral infections normally, her hair and skin pigment are normal, and immunoglobulins and complement levels are normal. Her neutrophils reach the abscesses and ingest bacteria normally but fail to kill them.
oneliner: 6F + repeated skin and liver abscesses (S aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia) + normal viral immunity and pigment + normal Igs and complement + neutrophils reach and ingest but do not kill → which step has failed?
ask: Which step of neutrophil function is defective?

options.B: Chemotaxis toward the site of infection
options.C: Adhesion to endothelium through CD18 integrins

whyNot.A: **Chediak-Higashi**: partial albinism and giant granules; her **pigment is normal**
whyNot.B: Cells **reach the abscesses**, so they migrate
whyNot.C: **Leukocyte adhesion deficiency** gives infections **without pus**; she forms abscesses
whyNot.D: Stated as **normal** in the stem

answer: NADPH oxidase defect: no superoxide for killing catalase-positive organisms (chronic granulomatous disease)
why: Phagocytes **ingest normally** but lack the **NADPH oxidase respiratory burst**, so no **superoxide and hydrogen peroxide** form. **Catalase-positive bacteria** destroy their own peroxide, so the cells cannot borrow it; infections with these organisms recur and form **granulomas**.

idea.rule: Phagocytes that ingest but cannot kill = oxidative burst failure.
also: Test with dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry (NBT historically)
X-linked (gp91phox) is most common; autosomal forms exist
Organisms: S aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia, Nocardia, Aspergillus

stem: A 44-year-old man with recurrent sinus infections and chronic giardiasis is given fresh frozen plasma for a bleeding episode. Within minutes he develops wheeze, hives, abdominal cramps and hypotension. Serum IgA is undetectable and IgG and IgM are normal.
oneliner: 44M + recurrent sinus infections + chronic giardiasis + fresh frozen plasma + within minutes wheeze, hives, cramps, hypotension + IgA undetectable, IgG and IgM normal → what reacted?
ask: Which reaction most likely caused his symptoms?

options.A: Donor leukocyte antibodies activating recipient neutrophils in the lungs
options.B: Recipient antibodies against donor red cell antigens
options.C: Recipient IgE or IgG against donor IgA in the plasma
options.D: Recipient T-cell release of interferon gamma

whyNot.A: **TRALI** gives noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, not hives and cramps in an **IgA-deficient** host
whyNot.B: Plasma **contains no red cells**
whyNot.D: A **delayed** response, not minutes
whyNot.E: Not a mechanism of **immediate** transfusion reactions

answer: Anti-IgA antibodies in selective IgA deficiency react with donor IgA
why: Patients with **selective IgA deficiency** can **make anti-IgA antibodies** after exposure. **Plasma contains IgA**, which these antibodies bind, causing **mast-cell activation and anaphylaxis** within minutes. Future products should be **from IgA-deficient donors or washed**.
chain: Immune complexes and mast cell activation

idea.rule: IgA-deficient patients can react to IgA in any blood product.
also: Selective IgA deficiency: sinopulmonary infections, giardiasis, celiac
Treat with epinephrine, then use washed cells or IgA-deficient donors
Most are asymptomatic

stem: Researchers translate the mRNA of a secreted hormone in a cell-free system with no microsomes, and the protein is larger than the hormone purified from culture medium. When rough endoplasmic reticulum microsomes are present during translation, the product has the size of the secreted hormone.
oneliner: Cell-free translation of secreted hormone mRNA + larger protein without microsomes + secreted size when RER microsomes present → what process shortens it?
ask: Which process most likely explains the shorter product?

options.B: Cleavage of the N-terminal signal peptide by signal peptidase in the ER
options.E: Removal of a propeptide by furin in secretory vesicles

whyNot.A: Would make the protein **larger**, not smaller
whyNot.C: Would give **heterogeneous fragments**, not one size
whyNot.D: Adds **mass** and ties it to the membrane
whyNot.E: Occurs **later, after the ER**; the shift is seen with ER microsomes alone

answer: Signal peptide removed in the rough ER, so the mature protein is shorter than the translated product
why: The **N-terminal signal sequence** is recognized by **SRP**, which brings the ribosome to the **RER**. **Signal peptidase** inside the ER lumen **cuts it off**, so the mature secreted protein is **shorter than the primary translation product**.
chain: SRP delivers ribosome to the RER

idea.rule: Secretory and membrane proteins are synthesized with a removable address label.
also: Defective SRP or signal sequence: protein stays in cytosol
I-cell disease: lacks mannose-6-phosphate tag
Prohormone cleavage (insulin) happens later in vesicles

stem: A 4-year-old boy drinks a cleaning solvent from the garage and develops liver and kidney failure from necrosis of hepatocytes and renal tubular cells. With supportive care, both organs gradually recover normal structure over the next weeks.
oneliner: 4M + solvent ingestion + hepatocyte and tubular cell necrosis + full recovery → how are lost cells replaced?
ask: Which of the following best explains how the lost cells are replaced?

options.B: Differentiation of a resident stem cell reserve
options.C: Shortened G1 in cells that are already cycling
options.D: Re-entry of resting cells from G0 into the cell cycle

whyNot.A: Scar is the outcome in **permanent** tissues such as cardiac muscle; his organs recover normal structure
whyNot.B: Used by **labile** tissues (skin, gut), which renew continuously; hepatocytes and tubular cells mostly regenerate themselves
whyNot.C: These are **not continuously cycling** cells; they are resting at baseline
whyNot.E: That is the **end of cycling**, not a way to make new cells

answer: Quiescent (stable) cells in G0 re-enter G1 and divide
why: Hepatocytes and tubular cells are **stable cells**: they sit in **G0** but are triggered by growth factors to enter **G1** after injury. This restores tissue with intact architecture, provided the framework is preserved.

idea.rule: Stable cells regenerate by re-entering the cycle from G0; permanent cells cannot.
also: Labile: skin, gut epithelium, marrow (always cycling)
Stable: liver, kidney tubules, endothelium, fibroblasts
Permanent: neurons, cardiac myocytes (heal by scar)
Liver needs an intact stroma to regenerate

stem: In an experiment, cultured fibroblasts are synchronised and sampled at intervals. Just before the cells enter mitosis, the kinase CDK1 is activated by binding to its partner cyclin, which has accumulated in the preceding phase.
oneliner: Synchronised cultured cells + CDK1 activated just before mitosis by its partner cyclin → in which phase is that cyclin synthesised?
ask: In which phase of the cell cycle is this cyclin mainly synthesised?

whyNot.A: G0 is the **resting** state with no cycling machinery being built
whyNot.B: G1 makes **cyclin D and E** for the G1/S checkpoint, not the mitotic cyclin
whyNot.C: S phase is DNA replication, driven by **cyclin A / E-CDK2**
whyNot.E: Mitotic cyclin is **degraded** during M, which allows exit from mitosis

answer: G2 (cyclin B accumulates and activates CDK1)
why: The cyclin that partners with **CDK1** is **cyclin B**, synthesised during **G2**. Its rise triggers the **G2/M transition**, and its degradation at the end of mitosis lets cells exit.

idea.rule: Each cell-cycle transition is driven by its own cyclin-CDK pair; cyclin B-CDK1 drives G2 to M.
also: Cyclin D-CDK4/6 and cyclin E-CDK2: G1 to S
Cyclin A-CDK2: S phase
p21 and p27 block CDKs
Rb phosphorylation releases E2F for G1/S

stem: A 30-year-old man is admitted after a crush injury to his leg. On the next morning, his plasma fibrinogen is 650 mg/dL (normal 200-400). His platelet count and prothrombin time are normal, and he has no abnormal bleeding.
oneliner: 30M + crush injury + next-day fibrinogen 650 (raised) + normal platelets and PT + no bleeding → why fibrinogen is high?
ask: Which of the following best explains the high fibrinogen?

options.B: Increased hepatic synthesis driven by inflammatory cytokines

whyNot.A: Consumption would **lower** fibrinogen; platelets and PT are normal
whyNot.C: Would raise **all plasma proteins** modestly, not double fibrinogen
whyNot.D: Causes **vasodilation and edema**, not a rise in plasma fibrinogen
whyNot.E: Platelet counts are **normal**, and plasma fibrinogen would not rise this way

answer: IL-6 and IL-1 drive the liver to make fibrinogen (acute-phase response)
why: Tissue injury releases **IL-6, IL-1 and TNF**, which make hepatocytes **upregulate acute-phase proteins** (fibrinogen, CRP, ferritin, hepcidin) and **lower albumin**. The fibrinogen rise is a **positive acute-phase** change.

idea.rule: IL-6 (with IL-1, TNF) makes the liver raise positive acute-phase proteins and lower albumin.
also: CRP and serum amyloid A
Ferritin and hepcidin (anemia of chronic disease)
Fibrinogen (raises ESR via rouleaux)
Albumin and transferrin fall (negative reactants)

stem: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is receiving her first rituximab infusion. After 45 minutes, she develops fever to 38.8 °C, chills and muscle aches. BP is normal, and she has no rash, wheeze, lip swelling or throat tightness.
oneliner: 52F + RA + 45 min into first rituximab infusion + fever, chills, myalgias + normal BP + no urticaria, wheeze or angioedema → mechanism?
ask: Which of the following best explains her reaction?

options.A: Type I hypersensitivity with mast cell degranulation
options.B: Immune complex deposition in small vessels
options.E: Cytokine release from B cells lysed by the antibody

whyNot.A: No **urticaria, wheeze, angioedema or hypotension**
whyNot.B: Takes **7-14 days** (serum sickness), not minutes
whyNot.C: Would cause **thrombosis or thrombocytopenia**, not fever and myalgia
whyNot.D: Takes **days** and presents with rash or induration

answer: Anti-CD20 lyses B cells and releases cytokines (cytokine-release reaction)
why: Rituximab binds **CD20**, and rapid **B cell lysis** releases **TNF, IL-6 and other cytokines**. This causes **fever, chills and myalgia** during the first infusion, **without** IgE features such as urticaria or bronchospasm.
chain: Rituximab binds CD20 on B cells

idea.rule: Infusion reaction without urticaria is cytokine release, not IgE anaphylaxis.
also: CAR-T cells: cytokine release syndrome (IL-6; tocilizumab)
Muromonab-CD3 (OKT3): first-dose cytokine release
Alemtuzumab (anti-CD52) first infusions

stem: A 31-year-old woman develops fever, hives, joint pain and swollen lymph nodes 9 days after starting a course of penicillin. Serum C3 is low and urinalysis shows mild proteinuria.
oneliner: 31F + 9 days after penicillin + fever, hives, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy + low C3 + mild proteinuria → which complement fragment causes the hives?
ask: Which of the following complement products most directly causes the histamine release behind her hives?

whyNot.A: Binds **Fc of immune complexes** to start the classical pathway
whyNot.B: An **opsonin**, coating complexes for phagocytosis
whyNot.C: Starts assembly of the **membrane attack complex**
whyNot.D: Causes **lysis** of cells, not histamine release

answer: C3a (an anaphylatoxin) triggers mast cell degranulation
why: Penicillin-antibody **immune complexes** (type III hypersensitivity) activate complement. **C3a and C5a** are **anaphylatoxins** that **degranulate mast cells**, releasing histamine and causing **urticaria**; complement consumption lowers **C3**.

idea.rule: C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins that degranulate mast cells.
also: C5a: strongest anaphylatoxin, also neutrophil chemotactic
C4a: weak anaphylatoxin
Anaphylatoxins add to urticaria in serum sickness and transfusion reactions

stem: Before a kidney transplant, lymphocytes from the donor are irradiated so they cannot divide, and are then cultured with the recipient's lymphocytes. Proliferation of the recipient's T cells is measured by thymidine uptake. The donor is HLA-DR3/DR6 and the recipient is HLA-DR3/DR4.
oneliner: Mixed lymphocyte reaction + irradiated donor cells (DR3/DR6) + recipient T cells (DR3/DR4) + proliferation measured → which donor DR molecule(s) are recognised?
ask: The proliferating recipient T cells are most likely responding to which donor HLA-DR molecule or molecules?

whyNot.A: The recipient **also carries DR3**, so it is self
whyNot.B: DR4 is on the **recipient**, not the donor
whyNot.D: DR3 is **shared** and is not foreign
whyNot.E: DR4 is **the recipient's own** type

answer: Recipient T cells react to the donor's foreign DR6
why: T cells **tolerate HLA molecules they carry** and respond to **non-self HLA**. The donor's DR3 is shared, so the only **foreign donor HLA-DR is DR6**. Irradiation stops donor cells dividing, so the **recipient's** response is what is measured.
chain: Irradiated donor cells present their HLA
Recipient T cells compare with their own HLA
DR3 is self, DR6 is foreign

idea.rule: Responder T cells proliferate against HLA types they do not carry.
also: Direct allorecognition: recipient T cells see intact donor MHC
Indirect: recipient APCs present donor peptides
Hyperacute rejection: preformed antibodies
HLA matching priority: DR, then B, then A

stem: A 31-year-old woman has joint pain, a facial rash over the cheeks, and pleuritic chest pain. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein with red cell casts. Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are positive and C3 and C4 are low. She has no urticaria or eosinophilia.
oneliner: 31F + arthralgia + malar rash + pleuritic pain + proteinuria with RBC casts + anti-dsDNA positive + low C3 and C4 → how is tissue injured?
ask: Which mechanism is most responsible for her organ injury?

options.A: Antibodies binding a fixed basement membrane antigen
options.C: Direct CD8 T cell killing of tissue cells
options.D: Circulating immune complexes depositing in tissues and activating complement
options.E: Th1 activation of macrophages forming granulomas

whyNot.A: **Anti-GBM disease**: linear deposits, lung and kidney, normal complement
whyNot.B: **Type I**: urticaria, eosinophilia and wheeze within minutes
whyNot.C: **Cell-mediated**: no complement consumption and no autoantibodies
whyNot.E: **Type IV**: granulomas, normal complement

answer: Type III hypersensitivity: immune complex deposition with complement consumption
why: **Anti-dsDNA** antibodies form **immune complexes** that **deposit in joints, skin, serosa and glomeruli**. They **fix complement**, so **C3 and C4 fall**, and neutrophils and macrophages injure the tissue: **type III hypersensitivity**.
chain: Deposit in glomeruli, skin, joints, serosa
Complement activated, C3 and C4 consumed

idea.rule: Lupus is the prototype of immune complex disease with low complement.
also: Type III also: serum sickness, PSGN, polyarteritis nodosa
Anti-Sm and anti-dsDNA are specific; ANA is sensitive
Anti-dsDNA titers track nephritis

stem: A 34-year-old woman has had a dry cough, night sweats and fatigue for 6 weeks. Chest imaging shows bilateral hilar lymph node enlargement. A cervical lymph node biopsy is taken. Acid-fast and fungal stains are negative. A photomicrograph of the node is shown.
oneliner: 34F + dry cough, sweats, fatigue 6 weeks + bilateral hilar adenopathy + node biopsy with negative AFB and fungal stains + photomicrograph shown → immune mechanism?
ask: Which immune mechanism best explains the lesion?

options.C: Antibody binding to cell surface antigens
options.D: Natural killer cell lysis of infected cells
options.E: CD4+ Th1 cell activation of macrophages

whyNot.A: **Type III**: neutrophilic vasculitis with complement consumption, not nodules
whyNot.B: **Type I**: minutes after allergen, not a chronic nodal lesion
whyNot.C: **Type II**: cytotoxicity or receptor effects without granulomas
whyNot.D: Kills cells directly but **does not form granulomas**

answer: Type IV hypersensitivity: Th1 cells make IFN-gamma, activating macrophages into epithelioid granulomas
why: **Th1 CD4 cells** respond to an unknown antigen and secrete **IFN-gamma**, which turns macrophages into **epithelioid cells and giant cells**. They form **noncaseating granulomas**, a **delayed-type (type IV)** reaction; negative stains exclude TB and fungi.
chain: Noncaseating granuloma in nodes and lung

idea.rule: Granulomas are delayed-type hypersensitivity driven by Th1 cells and IFN-gamma.
also: Sarcoidosis: high ACE, hypercalcemia from macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase
Tuberculosis: caseating granulomas
Crohn disease and berylliosis also form granulomas

image.prompt: H&E photomicrograph of a lymph node showing several well-formed, tightly packed granulomas made of epithelioid histiocytes with scattered multinucleated giant cells, rimmed by lymphocytes, with no central necrosis and surrounding preserved lymphoid tissue. No text or labels.

stem: Cultured cardiac myocytes are kept in a hypoxic chamber for several hours. A fluorescent indicator shows the cytosolic calcium has risen until it equals the extracellular concentration. Normally the gradient is about 10,000-fold. Propidium iodide, a dye that cannot cross intact membranes, now stains the nuclei.
oneliner: Cultured cardiomyocytes + hours of hypoxia + cytosolic Ca²⁺ equals outside + propidium iodide enters → what is the state of the cells?
ask: Which of the following best describes the state of these cells?

whyNot.A: Membrane integrity is **still intact** in reversible injury
whyNot.B: Cells grow **in size** under load, with normal membranes
whyNot.D: Cells **shrink** with intact membranes
whyNot.E: Replacement by another **mature cell type**; membranes intact

answer: Irreversible injury with cell death
why: A normal cell keeps cytosolic calcium about **10,000-fold below** the outside. **Loss of the gradient and entry of propidium iodide** mean the **plasma membrane has failed**, the mark of irreversible injury.
chain: Membrane pumps fail and the membrane is damaged

idea.rule: Membrane failure with calcium influx marks the point of no return in cell injury.
also: Prolonged ischemia of myocardium
Reperfusion injury with calcium overload
Mitochondrial permeability transition
Leaky membranes release troponin and CK-MB

stem: Rats have a standard 6-mm dermal punch wound on the back. Half receive a daily topical growth factor, basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF), and half receive vehicle alone. On day 7 the wounds treated with bFGF are redder and more granular than those in controls. Tissue sections are taken.
oneliner: Rat dermal wounds + daily topical bFGF vs vehicle + day 7 wounds redder and granular → what is increased in sections?
ask: Which of the following is most likely increased in the treated wounds?

whyNot.A: Neutrophils dominate the **first 1 to 2 days**; by day 7 the redness reflects **new vessels**
whyNot.C: **Matrix breakdown** is not what FGF drives in healing
whyNot.D: Characteristic of **allergic and parasitic** responses
whyNot.E: Typical of **granulomatous** responses to foreign material

answer: Increased number of capillaries (angiogenesis in granulation tissue)
why: Around day 7 healing wounds fill with **granulation tissue**: new capillaries and fibroblasts in loose matrix. bFGF and VEGF **stimulate endothelial proliferation and sprouting**, so treated wounds are redder and richer in vessels. The same pink granular tissue is seen in a healing surgical incision at two weeks.
chain: Granulation tissue is richer in vessels

idea.rule: Granulation tissue is new capillaries plus fibroblasts; VEGF and FGF drive angiogenesis.
also: VEGF in tumors and wound repair
Pink, soft, granular tissue in healing surgical wounds
Hypoxia induces VEGF through HIF-1
Infantile hemangioma has high VEGF/FGF activity

stem: Cultured fibroblasts are given a dose of ionizing radiation. Over the next day the cells shrink, their membranes form blebs, and fragments are taken up by neighboring cells with no release of inflammatory mediators. Membranes remain intact and p53 is elevated.

why: The first sting made **IgE** that coated mast cells through **Fc-epsilon receptors**. On re-exposure the allergen **cross-links neighboring IgE**, and **preformed histamine** is released within minutes.
chain: First sting: Th2 help makes venom-specific IgE
IgE binds Fc-epsilon receptors on mast cells (sensitization)
Second sting: allergen cross-links adjacent IgE

idea.rule: Type I hypersensitivity needs prior sensitization, then allergen bridging IgE on the mast cell.
also: Penicillin or peanut anaphylaxis
Allergic rhinitis and asthma (early phase)
Urticaria after shellfish
Latex allergy

stem: In a culture experiment, natural killer cells are mixed with tumor cells that have lost all class I MHC expression. No antibody or serum is added. Within hours the tumor cells shrink, their nuclei fragment and DNA ladders appear, but the cell membranes stay intact until late.
oneliner: Experiment: NK cells + class I MHC-negative tumor cells, no antibody or serum → targets shrink with fragmented DNA. Killing mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism do the NK cells use to kill the tumor cells?

options.A: Engulfment and digestion of the tumor cell by the NK cell
options.B: Assembly of C5b-C9 pores in the tumor cell membrane
options.C: Respiratory burst with release of superoxide
options.D: Release of perforin and granzymes that trigger apoptosis
options.E: Antibody-coated targets removed by splenic macrophages

whyNot.A: NK cells are **not phagocytes**; the targets were killed from outside
whyNot.B: **No serum** was added, so there is no complement to build the membrane attack complex
whyNot.C: Targets show **DNA ladders with membranes intact**, which is apoptosis, not oxidative injury; the burst belongs to neutrophils and macrophages
whyNot.E: **No antibody** was added; macrophage removal of coated cells needs IgG

answer: Perforin pores plus granzymes entering the target (apoptosis)
why: NK cells find cells that **lack class I MHC**. They release **perforin**, which punches pores, and **granzymes**, serine proteases that enter and activate **caspases**, so the target dies by **apoptosis**.
chain: Tumor cell loses class I MHC
Inhibitory NK receptors get no signal
NK cell releases perforin and granzymes
Caspases activate: apoptosis with DNA fragmentation

idea.rule: NK cells and CD8+ T cells kill the same way: perforin makes the door, granzyme does the killing.
also: CD8+ T cells kill virus-infected cells with perforin and granzyme
Fas-Fas ligand is the second, receptor-based route to apoptosis
NK cells also do ADCC through CD16 (Fc-gamma receptor III)
NK cells are CD16+ and CD56+

stem: In a laboratory experiment, bacteria are incubated with fresh serum and then mixed with neutrophils; they are engulfed far faster than bacteria kept without serum. When one complement fragment is removed from the serum, the faster engulfment disappears, although the serum still attracts neutrophils strongly.
oneliner: Experiment: serum-treated bacteria engulfed faster by neutrophils; removing one complement fragment abolishes it, but serum still attracts neutrophils → which fragment?
ask: Which complement fragment was removed?

whyNot.A: **C3a** is an anaphylatoxin that degranulates mast cells; it does not coat bacteria to **speed engulfment**
whyNot.B: **C5a** is the main chemotactic fragment, and the serum **still attracts neutrophils**, so C5a is present
whyNot.D: **C5b-C9** lyses the target; it does not **speed engulfment**
whyNot.E: **C4a** is a weak anaphylatoxin and does not coat bacteria for engulfment

answer: C3b
why: **C3b** covalently coats the microbe and is the major complement **opsonin**. Phagocytes bind it through **CR1** and ingest the particle faster.
chain: Complement activated on the bacterial surface

idea.rule: Match the fragment to the job: C3b opsonizes, C5a attracts, C3a and C5a inflame, C5b-C9 lyses.
also: C3a and C5a: anaphylatoxins
C5a: neutrophil chemotaxis
C5b-C9: membrane attack complex (Neisseria risk if deficient)
IgG also opsonizes, through Fc-gamma receptors

stem: A 16-year-old boy has sneezing and itchy eyes every spring. Skin testing is positive to grass pollen, and his blood eosinophils and serum IgE are raised. Allergen-specific IgE first appeared after his earliest exposures to grass pollen.
oneliner: 16M + spring sneezing and itchy eyes + positive grass skin test + high eosinophils and IgE → which cytokine directed the switch to IgE?
ask: Which cytokine, made by helper T cells, directed his B cells to class switch to IgE?

whyNot.A: **IFN-gamma** (Th1) favors IgG and opposes switching to **IgE**
whyNot.B: **TGF-beta** favors IgA switching
whyNot.C: **IL-2** is a T-cell growth factor, not an isotype director, so it cannot explain the **IgE**
whyNot.D: **IL-17** (Th17) recruits neutrophils; it does not drive the **IgE and eosinophil** picture here

answer: IL-4 (with CD40L help)
why: Allergens drive **Th2** cells. **IL-4**, with **CD40-CD40L** contact, tells B cells to switch to **IgE**; **IL-5** adds eosinophilia.
chain: Allergen taken up by dendritic cells
Naive CD4+ T cells become Th2
Th2 releases IL-4 and expresses CD40L

idea.rule: The cytokine decides the isotype: IL-4 gives IgE, IFN-gamma gives IgG, TGF-beta gives IgA.
also: IL-5 drives eosinophils and helps IgA
IL-4 also turns naive CD4+ cells into Th2 cells
IFN-gamma favors opsonizing IgG
CD40L deficiency blocks all switching (hyper-IgM)

stem: In an experiment, a CD4+ T-cell clone is shown to recognize a peptide of influenza hemagglutinin sitting in class II HLA on a B cell. The B cell had captured the viral protein from outside with its surface immunoglobulin.
oneliner: Experiment: CD4+ clone sees influenza hemagglutinin peptide on class II HLA of a B cell that captured the protein from outside → where did peptide meet HLA?
ask: In which cell compartment did the peptide combine with the class II HLA molecule?

whyNot.A: The **ER** loads peptide onto **class I**; class II there is blocked by invariant chain, and this clone sees **class II**
whyNot.C: **Cytosolic** peptides (proteasome) go to **class I**; this protein came **from outside**
whyNot.D: The Golgi **transports** class II toward the endosome but does not load the peptide
whyNot.E: No antigen is processed in the nucleus for HLA

answer: Endosome (late endosome or MIIC)
why: Class II HLA is made in the **rough ER** with **invariant chain** in its groove, and travels to an **acidic endosome**. There the invariant chain is cut to **CLIP**, **HLA-DM** swaps it for **peptide from endocytosed protein**.
chain: Class II made in ER with invariant chain
Vesicle fuses with endosome carrying engulfed antigen
Invariant chain cut down to CLIP
Complex goes to surface for CD4+ T cells

idea.rule: Class II sees outside antigens loaded in the endosome; class I sees inside antigens loaded in the ER.
also: Class I: cytosolic peptide, proteasome, TAP, ER
Class II is found on B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells
Bare lymphocyte syndrome type II: no class II, low CD4+
Cross-presentation lets dendritic cells load exogenous antigen on class I

stem: An investigator joins meningococcal capsular polysaccharide to several different compounds and injects each conjugate into mice. Anticapsular IgG is later measured. Polysaccharide alone gives only IgM with no memory, and the B cell takes in the whole conjugate through its polysaccharide-specific receptor.
oneliner: Experiment: meningococcal polysaccharide conjugated to different compounds in mice, anticapsular IgG measured; polysaccharide alone gives only IgM → which carrier raises IgG?
ask: Which carrier compound would most likely raise anticapsular IgG?

whyNot.A: A **sugar** gives no peptide for MHC II, so **no T-cell help**
whyNot.B: A **lipid** gives no peptide for class II, so no T-cell help and no IgG
whyNot.C: **Poly I:C** is a TLR3 ligand and adjuvant but **not a protein**, so no carrier peptide for T cells
whyNot.E: **LPS** can activate B cells directly but gives **no cognate T-cell help**

answer: A protein carrier such as tetanus toxoid
why: T cells recognize only **peptides on MHC II**. The B cell swallows the conjugate, presents **carrier peptide**, and **CD4+ T cells** give **CD40L and cytokine help**, producing **IgG** and memory.
chain: B cell binds polysaccharide, takes in the conjugate
Peptide on class II shown to CD4+ T cell
T cell gives CD40L and cytokines
Class switch to IgG, memory cells

idea.rule: Polysaccharides are T-independent; add a protein and the response becomes T-dependent.
also: Hib, pneumococcal and meningococcal conjugate vaccines
Pure polysaccharide vaccines work poorly under 2 years of age
Hapten-carrier effect: a small hapten raises antibody only when linked to a protein carrier
Polysaccharide alone gives mainly IgM and little memory

stem: A 3-month-old boy is given tetanus toxoid. His serum first shows IgM against the toxin, and a few weeks later IgG against the same toxin epitope with the same binding strength. The switch needed CD40-CD40L contact and the enzyme AID.
oneliner: 3-month-old boy + tetanus toxoid + IgM then IgG against the same epitope + CD40-CD40L and AID needed → which part of the immunoglobulin changed?
ask: Which part of the immunoglobulin molecule was replaced during the switch from IgM to IgG?

options.E: Both variable regions, giving a new specificity

whyNot.B: The **variable regions fix specificity**, and this specificity was unchanged
whyNot.C: The **heavy-chain variable region** is built by V(D)J joining and stays the same
whyNot.D: The **light chain** is not touched by class switching
whyNot.E: A change in the **variable regions** would give a new epitope, not the same one

answer: Heavy-chain constant region (isotype)
why: AID drives **switch recombination**, which cuts out the Cmu segment and joins the same **VDJ** to **Cgamma**. Only the **heavy-chain constant region** changes, so **antigen specificity stays the same**.
chain: B cell makes IgM with a given VDJ
CD40L plus cytokines signal the B cell
AID creates breaks in switch regions
Same epitope specificity, new effector function

idea.rule: Isotype switching changes the effector function; V(D)J rearrangement and hypermutation change the binding.
also: Somatic hypermutation (also AID) raises affinity, in the variable region
Hyper-IgM: CD40L, CD40 or AID defect, normal or high IgM, low IgG, IgA, IgE
IgM and IgD are made together by alternative RNA splicing, not by switching
Switching deletes the DNA between, so it cannot go back

stem: A 45-year-old woman who has had three pregnancies and a blood transfusion receives a deceased-donor kidney. Within minutes of the vascular clamps being released, the graft turns mottled and blue, and urine output stops. Biopsy shows neutrophils in the vessels, fibrinoid necrosis and thrombi.
oneliner: 45F + prior pregnancies and transfusion + kidney graft mottled and cyanotic within minutes of reperfusion + neutrophils, fibrinoid necrosis, thrombi → which mechanism destroys it?
ask: Which immune mechanism is destroying the graft?

options.A: Recipient T cells infiltrating the tubules
options.B: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissue
options.C: Preformed recipient antibodies binding graft endothelium and fixing complement
options.D: Slow intimal fibrosis from repeated low-grade injury

whyNot.A: **Acute cellular rejection** needs T-cell priming over **days to weeks**, not minutes
whyNot.B: **GVHD** is donor lymphocytes attacking the host's skin, gut and liver, not her graft failing **within minutes**
whyNot.D: **Chronic rejection** takes months to years and is gradual
whyNot.E: **Drug toxicity** does not give neutrophils and thrombi minutes after reperfusion

answer: Type II hypersensitivity: preformed antibodies and complement
why: Prior **pregnancies and transfusions** sensitize her to **HLA** antigens. **Preformed antibodies** bind graft endothelium within minutes, **fix complement**, and cause **thrombosis and ischemic necrosis**.
chain: Pregnancy or transfusion exposes her to donor-type HLA
Antibodies bind graft endothelium at reperfusion
Thrombosis, fibrinoid necrosis, graft loss in minutes

idea.rule: Hyperacute rejection is a type II reaction with preformed antibody, so it is immediate and untreatable.
also: ABO incompatibility causes the same picture
Prevented by crossmatch and ABO matching
Acute rejection: T cells (tubulitis) or antibody (vasculitis), weeks
Graft-versus-host disease: donor T cells attack the host

stem: A 52-year-old man had a kidney transplant 6 years ago. His creatinine has crept up over a year despite good adherence to his immunosuppressants. He has no fever and the graft is not tender. A biopsy shows graft arteries with narrowed lumens, tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis, with few lymphocytes in the tubules.
oneliner: 52M + kidney transplant 6 years ago + slowly rising creatinine, no fever or tenderness + biopsy: narrowed graft arteries, tubular atrophy, fibrosis, little tubulitis → which mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the slow loss of graft function?

options.A: Preformed antibodies fixing complement on graft endothelium
options.B: Acute T-cell attack on tubular epithelium (tubulitis)
options.D: Ascending bacterial infection of the graft
options.E: Smoldering alloimmune injury driving intimal proliferation in graft arteries

whyNot.A: **Hyperacute rejection** destroys the graft within **minutes** of reperfusion, not after 6 years
whyNot.B: **Acute cellular rejection** gives a sudden rise, and his biopsy shows **few lymphocytes in the tubules**
whyNot.C: **GVHD** damages the host's skin, gut and liver; here the **graft itself** is failing
whyNot.D: Infection would give **fever and a tender graft**; he has **neither**

answer: Chronic rejection: low-grade alloimmune injury causing graft arteriosclerosis and fibrosis
why: Years of low-grade **T-cell and antibody** injury drive **smooth muscle proliferation**, giving **intimal thickening (graft arteriosclerosis)**. The graft becomes **ischemic**, with **tubular atrophy and fibrosis**.
chain: Repeated low-grade immune injury to graft vessels
Ischemia, tubular atrophy, fibrosis, creatinine rises

idea.rule: Chronic rejection is a slow vascular and fibrotic process, and it does not respond to more immunosuppression.
also: Chronic lung rejection: bronchiolitis obliterans
Chronic heart rejection: coronary allograft vasculopathy
Chronic liver rejection: vanishing bile ducts
Acute cellular rejection is reversible with steroids

stem: Mice that lack a single eosinophil-specific cationic protein are infected with filarial worms. They make high IgE titers and have many eosinophils, yet cannot clear the worms, which are far too large to engulf.
oneliner: Experiment: mice lacking one eosinophil protein + filarial worms + high IgE and eosinophils yet worms persist, too large to engulf → how do eosinophils kill the worm?
ask: Which mechanism normally lets eosinophils kill the parasite?

options.A: Phagocytosis followed by a respiratory burst
options.B: Lysis by the complement membrane attack complex
options.C: NK-cell killing of cells that lack class I MHC
options.D: IgE-coated worm triggering release of toxic eosinophil granule proteins
options.E: CD8+ T-cell killing of cells showing peptide on class I MHC

whyNot.A: The worm is **too large to engulf**, so phagocytosis is impossible
whyNot.B: Complement needs no eosinophils, yet losing **one eosinophil protein** alone lets the worms survive
whyNot.C: **NK cells** kill host cells that lack class I; the target here is an **extracellular worm**
whyNot.E: **CD8+ T cells** kill infected host cells, not an **extracellular worm**

answer: IgE-dependent cellular cytotoxicity: eosinophils release major basic protein onto the worm
why: **IgE** coats the worm, and eosinophils bind it through **Fc-epsilon receptors**. They degranulate, releasing **major basic protein** onto the worm surface, which is **toxic** to it. **IL-5** drives their production.
chain: Th2 cells release IL-5 and IL-4
IL-5 expands eosinophils, IL-4 gives IgE
Eosinophils bind IgE through Fc receptors
Major basic protein released: worm damaged

idea.rule: Helminths are too big to eat, so IgE plus eosinophils attack from outside.
also: Eosinophilia points to helminths and allergy
Mast cell degranulation also expels worms
NK cells do ADCC with IgG through CD16
Eosinophils also appear in asthma and drug reactions

stem: A 6-month-old boy has recurrent pneumonia, oral thrush and failure to thrive. Flow cytometry shows no T or B cells but normal NK cells. Southern blot of his lymphocyte DNA shows only germline-size bands with immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor probes, meaning no gene rearrangement occurs.
oneliner: 6-month-old boy + recurrent pneumonia, thrush, failure to thrive + no T or B cells, normal NK cells + germline-size bands, no receptor rearrangement → which enzyme does the cutting?
ask: Which enzyme normally performs the DNA cutting step that is missing in this infant?

whyNot.B: **TdT** only adds random nucleotides at the joints; the **cutting by RAG** comes first
whyNot.C: **AID** acts later, in mature B cells, for switching and hypermutation
whyNot.D: **ADA** deficiency gives **low T, B and NK** cells (toxic metabolites)
whyNot.E: **BTK** loss gives **B-cell** absence only, with normal T cells

answer: RAG1/RAG2 (V(D)J recombinase)
why: **RAG1 and RAG2** cut DNA at **recombination signal sequences** to join **V, D and J** segments. Without them, **no B or T receptor** can be built, giving **T-B-NK+ SCID**.
chain: No DNA cutting at V, D, J segments
No functional TCR or immunoglobulin gene
No T or B cells, NK cells normal

idea.rule: RAG cuts and TdT adds; AID works later.
also: Omenn syndrome: leaky RAG mutation with erythroderma and eosinophilia
Artemis deficiency: radiosensitive T-B-NK+ SCID (cannot open the cut ends)
TdT adds N nucleotides at the joints, adding diversity
AID acts only after antigen, for switching and hypermutation

stem: A 5-month-old boy has fever, a severe dry cough and hypoxia, and bronchoalveolar lavage shows Pneumocystis jirovecii. His lymphocytes do not express HLA-DR, his CD8+ count is normal and his CD4+ count is very low. His immunoglobulin levels are also low.
oneliner: 5-month-old boy + Pneumocystis pneumonia + lymphocytes lack HLA-DR + low CD4+, normal CD8+ + low immunoglobulins → why is the CD4+ subset low?
ask: Which mechanism best explains his low CD4+ T-cell count?

options.A: Failed negative selection in the thymic medulla
options.C: Failure of positive selection of CD4+ cells without class II MHC in the thymic cortex
options.D: Absent thymus from failed third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development
options.E: Defective IL-2 receptor common gamma chain signaling

whyNot.A: Failed **negative selection** would leave **autoreactive** cells, not fewer CD4+ cells
whyNot.B: **HIV** kills CD4+ cells but would not remove **HLA-DR** from his lymphocytes
whyNot.D: **DiGeorge** lowers **all T cells**, but his **CD8+ count is normal**
whyNot.E: **X-linked SCID** lowers T and NK cells, **CD8+ would be low too**

answer: No class II MHC, so CD4+ cells are not positively selected
why: **CD4+** cells are **positively selected** in the **thymic cortex** only if their TCR binds **class II MHC**. With **no class II**, few CD4+ cells survive, helper help for B cells falls and **immunoglobulins drop**.
chain: Defect in class II MHC gene expression (CIITA, RFX)
No class II on thymic epithelium
CD4+ positive selection fails in cortex
Few CD4+ T cells, poor B-cell help

idea.rule: CD4 cells need class II to be selected; CD8 cells need class I.
also: Bare lymphocyte syndrome type I: no class I, low CD8+
CD4 = class II, CD8 = class I (the 'rule of 8': 8 = 2 x 4)
Thymic cortex: positive selection; medulla: negative selection
CIITA and RFX mutations cause MHC II deficiency

stem: In a cell-free assay, enzymes purified from healthy human neutrophils are mixed with NADPH and oxygen, but one enzyme is left out of the mix. Superoxide builds up, and hydrogen peroxide forms only slowly, at the rate expected with no enzyme help.
oneliner: Experiment: purified neutrophil enzymes + NADPH and oxygen, one enzyme left out → superoxide builds up, H2O2 forms only slowly → which enzyme is missing?
ask: Which enzyme was left out of the mix?

whyNot.A: **NADPH oxidase** makes superoxide, which **builds up** here
whyNot.B: **MPO** acts **after** peroxide is made, so leaving it out would not slow **H2O2 formation**
whyNot.C: **Catalase** breaks peroxide down; leaving it out would let peroxide **accumulate**, not form slowly
whyNot.D: **Glutathione peroxidase** also removes peroxide; its absence would not slow **H2O2 formation**

answer: Superoxide dismutase
why: **NADPH oxidase** makes **superoxide**, **superoxide dismutase** converts it to **hydrogen peroxide**, and **myeloperoxidase** turns peroxide plus chloride into **hypochlorous acid** (bleach).

idea.rule: Follow the burst step by step: oxidase, dismutase, myeloperoxidase.
also: Chronic granulomatous disease: NADPH oxidase defect, catalase-positive infections
Myeloperoxidase deficiency: no HOCl, usually mild
Catalase-positive organisms destroy their own peroxide in CGD
Dihydrorhodamine flow test detects the burst

stem: A 12-year-old girl cut her left palm on a kitchen knife 4 days ago, and the wound was cleaned and sutured. Healing is on track, and fibroblasts are now migrating into the wound to begin granulation tissue.
oneliner: 12F + sutured knife cut to the palm 4 days ago + fibroblasts now migrating into the wound → which factor guides their migration?
ask: Which factor is most instrumental in guiding fibroblast migration into the wound?

whyNot.A: **Collagen** is laid down **after** fibroblasts arrive; at day 4 they are still **migrating**
whyNot.C: **Heparin** is a mast cell anticoagulant; it gives fibroblasts no track to **migrate** along
whyNot.D: **Plasminogen** becomes plasmin and clears fibrin; it does not guide **migrating** cells
whyNot.E: **Immunoglobulin** fights microbes; it plays no part in fibroblast **migration**

answer: Fibronectin
why: In the **provisional matrix** **fibronectin** binds fibroblast **integrins**, giving a **scaffold for migration**. Fibroblasts then lay down **type III collagen**, later replaced by **type I**.
chain: Injury: platelets and fibrin plug form
Fibronectin deposited in the provisional matrix

idea.rule: Fibronectin is the road, fibroblasts the traffic, collagen the final surface.
also: Type III collagen first, replaced by type I
TGF-beta stimulates fibroblasts and collagen
Myofibroblasts contract the wound through alpha-smooth muscle actin
Vitamin C is needed for collagen cross-linking

stem: A 37-year-old woman who received a deceased-donor kidney 3 months ago has a rise in serum creatinine from 1.1 to 2.0 mg/dL and mild graft tenderness. Her tacrolimus trough is low because she missed doses. A biopsy shows lymphocytes within the tubular epithelium and beneath arterial endothelium, with no C4d deposition.
oneliner: 37F + deceased-donor kidney 3 months ago + rising creatinine + low tacrolimus + lymphocytes in tubules and under arterial endothelium, C4d negative → which mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism is most likely injuring the graft?

options.A: Preformed recipient antibody binding donor endothelium
options.B: Recipient T cells responding to donor MHC
options.C: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissues
options.D: Direct toxic injury from the calcineurin inhibitor
options.E: Slow intimal fibrosis of graft arteries

whyNot.A: Preformed antibody acts within **minutes to hours** and would leave **C4d**; this is 3 months out and **C4d negative**
whyNot.C: Donor-against-host disease hits **skin, gut and liver**; here the **graft** is the target
whyNot.D: Drug toxicity needs **high** levels; her tacrolimus is **low**
whyNot.E: Chronic fibrosis builds over **months to years**; this biopsy shows **lymphocytes in tubules**, not scarring

answer: Recipient T cells reacting to donor MHC: acute T-cell-mediated (cellular) rejection
why: **Months after transplant**, with **low drug levels** and **lymphocytes in the tubules and under arterial endothelium (tubulitis, endarteritis)**, the graft is being attacked by **recipient CD8 and CD4 T cells** that recognize **donor MHC**. **C4d negative** argues against antibody. It usually responds to higher immunosuppression and steroids.
chain: Calcineurin no longer blocked, so IL-2 is made
Recipient T cells expand against donor MHC
Lymphocytes invade tubules and arterial intima

idea.rule: Rejection by timing: hyperacute in minutes (antibody), acute within weeks to 6 months (T cells), chronic over months to years.
also: Hyperacute: preformed anti-donor antibody, fibrinoid necrosis and thrombosis
Acute antibody-mediated: C4d-positive capillaries
Chronic: vascular thickening and fibrosis in the graft
Naive hosts reject a first-set graft in about 10-14 days

note: Review: moved from phys to mech (ask named a diagnosis); options now five mechanisms; spot series already has rejection-naming cards.

stem: A researcher studies inflamed venules in a mouse. After an experimental treatment, neutrophils no longer slow down and tumble along the vessel wall. Cells that reach the wall can still stick firmly in other conditions. Rolling normally depends on weak, short-lived bonds, including ones with sialyl-Lewis X on leukocytes.
oneliner: Experiment: neutrophils stop rolling along venular wall after treatment + rolling uses weak transient bonds + sialyl-Lewis X on leukocytes → which adhesion molecules?
ask: Which family of adhesion molecules was most likely blocked?

whyNot.A: Integrin-ICAM binding is the **firm adhesion** step that follows rolling
whyNot.B: PECAM-1 mediates **transmigration**, after firm adhesion
whyNot.C: Cadherins bind **cell to cell** in tissue and are not the rolling molecules
whyNot.E: VCAM-1 and VLA-4 bind **firmly**, after rolling

answer: Selectins
why: Rolling uses **selectins**: endothelial **E- and P-selectin** (P-selectin is stored in Weibel-Palade bodies) and leukocyte **L-selectin** bind sialyl-Lewis X ligands with weak, transient bonds. **Integrin-ICAM** binding then gives firm adhesion, and PECAM-1 mediates transmigration.

idea.rule: Rolling = selectins, sticking = integrins, crossing = PECAM-1.
also: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1: defective CD18 integrin
Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2: absent sialyl-Lewis X
P-selectin is stored in Weibel-Palade bodies and platelet alpha granules
Delayed cord separation suggests LAD type 1

stem: A 38-year-old woman has a benign lump excised from the back of her neck, and the incision is sutured. Eight days later the wound is pink and slightly warm, with no pain, pus or drainage. A biopsy of the incision is taken.
oneliner: 38F + sutured neck incision + day 8 + pink, slightly warm, no pus → which histologic process?
ask: Which process best describes the predominant histology of the incision now?

options.D: Remodeling of type III to type I collagen

whyNot.A: Neutrophils dominate the **first 1 to 3 days**; this wound is 8 days old with **no pus**
whyNot.B: Granulomas need a persistent agent such as a **foreign body or mycobacteria**; this wound is healing simply
whyNot.C: Eosinophils mark **allergy or parasites**, nothing here
whyNot.D: Collagen remodeling continues for **months**; at **day 8** the wound is still proliferative

answer: Angiogenesis (granulation tissue)
why: About **3 days to 2 weeks** after injury the wound is in the **proliferative phase**: **granulation tissue** with new capillaries (VEGF, FGF), fibroblasts laying down **type III collagen**, and myofibroblasts. The new vessels give the **pink, warm** look without infection. Remodeling to **type I collagen** follows over months, and strength plateaus near 70 to 80 percent.
chain: Angiogenesis and fibroblasts: granulation tissue (about day 3 to 2 weeks)
Type III collagen laid down; myofibroblasts contract
Remodeling to type I collagen over months

idea.rule: The age of a wound predicts its histology: neutrophils, then granulation tissue, then collagen remodeling.
also: Days 1 to 3: neutrophils and fibrin clot
About 1 week: granulation tissue with angiogenesis
Weeks to months: type III replaced by type I collagen (zinc-dependent collagenases)
Unsutured wounds fill with more granulation tissue (secondary intention)

stem: In a cell-free translation system, a ribosome reaches a UAA codon in the A site while the growing peptide is attached to the tRNA in the P site. No tRNA in the mixture has an anticodon that pairs with UAA.
oneliner: Experiment: ribosome with UAA in A site + peptide on P-site tRNA + no tRNA pairs with UAA → what happens next?
ask: Which event most likely occurs next?

options.D: Release factor binds, then peptide hydrolysis
options.E: Peptidyl transfer onto an E-site tRNA

whyNot.A: No tRNA in the mixture can **pair with a stop codon**
whyNot.B: Follows a **peptide bond** being made, and no tRNA can enter the A site to make one
whyNot.C: That is **initiation**, at the 5' end, not at the stop codon
whyNot.E: The peptide is on the **P-site tRNA**; peptidyl transfer moves it to an A-site tRNA, never to the E site

answer: Release factor binds the stop codon and the peptide is hydrolyzed from the P-site tRNA
why: A **stop codon in the A site** is read by a **release factor**, not a tRNA. This triggers **hydrolysis of the bond** between the peptide and the P-site tRNA, freeing the polypeptide.
chain: Stop codon (UAA) enters the A site
Release factor binds instead of a tRNA

idea.rule: Stop codons are read by proteins (release factors), not by tRNAs.
also: UAA, UAG and UGA are the three stop codons
Nonsense mutations create an early stop codon and a truncated protein
Initiation uses eIF-4E on the 5' cap, termination uses release factors

stem: In a cell-line experiment, a secretory protein with an N-terminal hydrophobic signal sequence is made but stays in the cytosol attached to its ribosome and never reaches the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The cells are found to lack a ribonucleoprotein that normally binds the emerging signal sequence.
oneliner: Experiment: secretory protein with N-terminal signal sequence stuck on cytosolic ribosome + never reaches rough ER + ribonucleoprotein missing → which component is absent?
ask: Which component is most likely absent?

whyNot.A: Sorts lysosomal enzymes in the **Golgi**, a later step, and is not a ribonucleoprotein
whyNot.C: A small **protein tag** for proteasomal degradation, not a ribonucleoprotein
whyNot.D: A **vesicle coat** protein, not a ribonucleoprotein that reads signal sequences
whyNot.E: Carries proteins with **nuclear localization signals** into the nucleus, not to the ER

answer: Signal recognition particle
why: The **signal recognition particle** (protein plus 7SL RNA) binds the **N-terminal signal sequence** and docks the ribosome on the rough ER. Without it, the nascent secretory protein stays on a free ribosome in the cytosol.
chain: SRP binds it and pauses translation
SRP docks ribosome on rough ER
Chain threads into the ER lumen

idea.rule: Secretory proteins reach the ER cotranslationally because SRP reads their signal sequence.
also: Secreted and membrane proteins are made on rough ER
Cytosolic proteins are made on free ribosomes
Signal peptidase then cuts the signal sequence off, so the secreted protein is shorter than its mRNA predicts

stem: In a phase 1 trial of a new drug, several participants develop raised AST and ALT, and liver biopsy shows injury thought to come from oxidative damage. Investigators want a measurement in the biopsy tissue that would confirm oxidative stress.
oneliner: Experiment: phase 1 drug trial + raised AST and ALT + liver injury suspected oxidative → which measurement shows oxidative stress?
ask: Which finding would best support oxidative stress as the mechanism?

options.A: Higher microsomal cytochrome P450 content of hepatocytes
options.B: Higher state 3 respiration in isolated liver mitochondria
options.C: Higher serum ALT above the baseline value
options.D: Lower ratio of reduced to oxidized glutathione
options.E: Higher glycogen content of hepatocytes on staining

whyNot.A: Reflects **drug metabolism** capacity or induction, not antioxidant reserve
whyNot.B: Shows **ADP-stimulated** respiratory capacity, not antioxidant reserve
whyNot.C: Already **raised** in the stem and marks injury of any cause
whyNot.E: Reflects **energy storage**, not the redox state

answer: Decreased GSH to GSSG ratio
why: **Reduced glutathione** uses its **sulfhydryl group** to neutralize free radicals and peroxides, becoming GSSG. Oxidative stress uses up GSH, so a **falling GSH:GSSG ratio** marks it, while enzyme leak shows only injury.

idea.rule: A falling reduced-to-oxidized glutathione ratio is the marker of oxidative stress.
also: Glutathione reductase regenerates GSH using NADPH
NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway protects red cells (G6PD deficiency)
Acetaminophen overdose depletes glutathione
